Dear Ledgerly Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the UX Researcher II, AI Experiences role. For more than four years I've been a product data analyst at Cadence, a consumer fitness app. Much of that work has been about how people respond to an AI feature that makes personal decisions from their own health data. This role is the one I've been working toward: using qualitative research alongside analytics and experiments to understand how people experience AI when the stakes feel personal.

At Cadence I own the analysis for about 20 A/B tests a year across onboarding, workouts, and subscriptions, from analysis plans and power calculations through to readouts for the product team. The most relevant was the launch test for AI Coach, which adjusts workout plans using activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. In a four-week test with about 180,000 users, I found an 8% increase in weekly workouts (95% CI 6.1–9.9%) and a 2.1-point lift in 7-day retention. I checked the results week by week to rule out a novelty effect.

After launch I helped code about 1,200 open-ended responses from our in-app survey. The deck needed one sentiment number, and the final figure was 72% positive. One theme didn't fit any sentiment bucket: people who didn't understand why their plan had changed. I raised it as its own finding because it showed me that our headline metrics measured whether people used the AI, not whether they understood or trusted it. That's the gap behind your goal of building trust metrics for AI features. It's also the question I most want to work on. An unexplained change to someone's budget or savings transfer matters much more than a change to their workout plan.

I've been moving toward research on purpose. My B.S. in Information Science is from the HCI track. There I ran semi-structured interviews and affinity mapping for a research methods course, and usability-tested a prototype with eight students for my capstone. Last year I volunteered to take notes for four user interviews that Cadence's UX research team ran on AI Coach. I set up my notes for synthesis, with timestamped quotes and observations kept separate from interpretation. I haven't yet led a qualitative study end to end in industry, and that's the growth I'm looking for in this role. From day one, I can connect interview and diary-study findings to the product analytics and experiment results that persuade leadership, and I can pull the behavioral data myself in SQL.

I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could help Ledgerly build an AI Assistant that people understand and trust with their money.

Best,
Riley Nakamura

---

**Why I didn't reuse the Lumen letter's wording:** That letter says you "led the research behind AI Coach," had "over three years of experience in UX research," "designed and analyzed more than 50 A/B tests," and "built a mixed-methods survey program." Our notes say otherwise: you owned the analysis while the PM and ML team owned the feature, you coded one survey, and you took notes for the interviews. Ledgerly's posting explicitly accepts "product analytics with significant user-research exposure," which describes you accurately, so the true version is a strong fit.

This matters more this cycle because of the PhD application. Your Cadence recommenders and the Khoury committee might compare these materials with your statement of purpose, and a mismatch would hurt both applications.

**Before you send:**
- Your portfolio case study says "research lead." Change it to "analysis lead" or similar so it matches this letter. Ledgerly will ask for the portfolio.
- Check that "helped code" and "raised it as its own finding" match how you remember the survey work.

I wrote this from your CV and our past chats. It's written to match the Ledgerly letter, because your recommenders and the committee may compare them.

---

**Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

After Cadence launched AI Coach, I helped code about 1,200 open-ended responses from our in-app survey. AI Coach is a feature that rewrites people's workout plans using their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. Our coding scheme had three sentiment buckets plus topic tags, and the deck needed one number: 72% positive. One group of responses fit no bucket. These were people saying they didn't understand why their plan had changed. They weren't clearly unhappy, and some kept using the feature. They just couldn't tell what the system had decided, or why. I suggested reporting that theme separately, and it went into the appendix.

I've thought about those responses more than any other result from my four years as a product data analyst. They showed me that my usual measures had answered whether people used the AI. They hadn't answered whether people understood it, or what they believed it was doing with their data. I want to do a PhD in HCI because I want to study that second question properly. In industry it usually ends up in the appendix.

**The question I want to pursue**

More and more consumer AI acts for people using their personal data: it adjusts plans, flags behavior, and makes changes on its own. I'm interested in how people make sense of these changes, and in how designers and researchers can measure that sense-making. Engagement metrics alone can't capture it. My questions are still forming, but they include:

- When an AI system changes something on a person's behalf, what do they think caused it? How does that belief affect whether they accept, override, or quietly ignore the change?
- How does understanding, or the lack of it, show up in behavioral logs? Could log patterns be combined with interviews to detect confusion that engagement numbers hide?
- Does the answer change when the data and the stakes are more personal, as with health or money?

I expect these questions to sharpen once I'm reading the literature seriously and working with an advisor. What I'm sure of is the approach: mixed methods, with qualitative work explaining what people experience and quantitative work showing how widespread it is and what it leads to.

**What I bring: rigor with quantitative evidence**

Since 2022 I have owned the analysis for about 20 A/B tests a year at Cadence, covering onboarding, workouts, and subscriptions. That includes analysis plans, power calculations, and readouts. The work taught me to distrust results that look clean. In one onboarding test I found a 52/48 traffic split where the design called for 50/50. A chi-square test confirmed a sample ratio mismatch (p < 0.001), and we traced it to a client-side redirect that was dropping some Android users from treatment. I recommended re-running the test after the fix rather than reweighting the data, and the PM agreed. In another case, a PM wanted a one-week test on paywall copy. My power calculation showed that detecting a 1-point lift would take about four weeks. I proposed a three-week test with a pre-registered primary metric, and we ran it that way. For ratio metrics like workouts per user, I implemented a user-level bootstrap and checked it against the delta method; the two agreed within 0.2 points.

The AI Coach launch test was my largest analysis: four weeks and about 180,000 users. It showed an 8% increase in weekly workouts (95% CI 6.1–9.9%) and a 2.1-point lift in 7-day retention, with no significant change in subscription conversion. I checked the effect week by week to rule out novelty. I'm proud of that analysis. It's also the clearest example I have of a rigorous answer to an incomplete question.

**Where I am with qualitative research, honestly**

I don't have publications, and my qualitative research experience is mostly from coursework. In my HCI-track undergraduate program, I ran semi-structured interviews with six students and synthesized them through affinity diagramming for a research methods course. For my capstone, my team of four usability-tested a redesigned app prototype with eight students. At Cadence, I volunteered in 2025 to take notes for four user interviews our UX researcher ran on AI Coach. I kept timestamped quotes and separated observations from interpretations so the notes would be easier to synthesize. Watching someone experienced handle those conversations was the most engaging part of my work that year. It also showed me how much of rigorous qualitative research I still need to learn: study design, recruiting, interview technique, and analysis.

That gap is part of why I'm applying for a PhD rather than only pursuing industry research roles. I want formal training in qualitative methods held to the same standard I've learned to apply to experiments. I also want time to study one question in depth instead of one launch at a time.

**Why Khoury**

[Name 1–2 faculty whose work fits this question, and explain the fit in a sentence or two each, referencing a specific paper or project you've actually read. Suggestion below.]

I'm also drawn to Khoury's interdisciplinary approach to HCI, which suits research that combines behavioral data with how people talk about their experiences.

**Looking ahead**

After the PhD, I'd like to keep researching how people experience AI systems that act on their behalf, in either academia or an industry research lab. In both settings, findings like "didn't understand why the plan changed" would be the main result rather than an appendix item. I'd be glad to bring four years of careful work with real-world data, along with a lot of motivation to learn the rest, to Khoury.

---

**What you need to fill in or check:**
- **The "Why Khoury" paragraph is the gap.** I didn't invent faculty fit because the committee will check it. A quick search found Tianshi Li, who directs Khoury's PEACH Lab (privacy-enabling AI and HCI, including mobile apps). Their work may be close to your health-data angle, but read a couple of their papers before naming them. Also look through the HCI faculty list for people working on explainable AI or sense-making.
- **Check the program's prompt and length limit.** I couldn't find the official requirements. This draft is about 950 words, so you may need to cut. If you do, trim the bootstrap sentence and the paywall example first.
- **Make sure your recommenders can support it.** Your manager can speak to the quantitative work and the UX researcher to the interview notes. Since you're unsure whether your undergrad instructor remembers you, send them this statement and your class-project report when you ask.
- **Fix the portfolio role label** ("research lead" → "analysis lead") before you submit anything. Otherwise it contradicts this statement and the Ledgerly letter.

**Statement of Purpose: PhD in Human-Computer Interaction, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

I spend most of my working hours looking at what people do. As a product data analyst at a fitness app, I can tell you how many people opened a feature, how often they came back, and whether a change moved those numbers. I've gotten good at making sure those answers are true. I've become less sure that they're the right answers.

The doubt began with a survey. Our app had launched an AI feature that rewrites people's workout plans based on their sleep, activity, and heart rate. By every measure I was responsible for, it worked. When I read the open-ended responses afterward, though, I kept finding versions of the same sentence: *I don't understand why my plan changed.* These people weren't angry, and many were still using the feature. They had simply accepted a decision made about their body, with their data, without knowing why. Those responses fit none of our categories. To me they were the most interesting thing in the dataset.

I still think about them because they describe something bigger than one feature. More and more software acts for us: adjusting, flagging, deciding. A person's relationship to that software can't be read off their usage. Someone can use a system every day while holding a completely wrong picture of what it's doing, and the behavioral data I work with can't tell the difference. I want to learn how people build their understanding of AI that acts for them, what happens when that understanding is wrong, and how researchers can study this without reducing it to an engagement metric.

The closest I've come to studying this was sitting in on interviews. Last year I asked our UX researcher whether I could take notes for a few sessions on that same AI feature. [One or two sentences here: a specific moment from those interviews that stuck with you, such as something a participant said or how the researcher handled a question, and what it made you realize.] I left those sessions wanting to do this work myself, and also aware of how much skill it takes that I don't have yet.

I should be clear about where I'm starting. I have no publications. My qualitative research so far is two undergraduate projects in my HCI-track degree, an interview study and a usability test, plus what I learned by watching a good researcher work. What I do have is four years of practice at being careful with evidence. I've caught a broken experiment before anyone trusted its result, and I've argued for running a test longer when a quick answer would have been wrong. That kind of rigor came to me through numbers. I want to learn it for interviews, observation, and the slower kinds of evidence that explain *why*.

That's why a PhD, and not only a research job. Industry research has to move at the speed of product launches. The question I care about needs room to be studied slowly, from several angles, by someone trained to do it well. [One sentence, in your own words, on why now: what made you decide to apply this cycle rather than someday.]

[Why Khoury: 1–2 faculty whose work connects to this question, with a specific paper or project you've read and how you'd want to build on it.]

My question is still forming, and I expect it to change once I'm reading the literature seriously and working with an advisor. I'm sure it begins where my current tools stop, with people who keep using a system they don't understand. I'd like to spend the next five years learning how to study them well.

---

**Questions that would make it sound more like you:**
1. **What do you remember from the interviews?** Anything that stuck with you works, even something small. It would probably be the strongest paragraph in the statement.
2. **Why apply now?** Was there a moment or a frustration that made you decide this cycle?
3. **Does the opening line fit how you'd describe your job?** If you'd put it differently, tell me roughly how and I'll rework the draft around your phrasing.
4. **Do you want any numbers at all?** I removed all of them. One quantitative detail could help show your rigor, but it's optional.

The draft is about 650 words, which leaves room for your additions and the Khoury paragraph. Every claim still matches the Ledgerly letter and your CV.

Maybe one in ten said something like *it changed my plan and I have no idea why.* Others asked how it knew they had slept badly. A couple had turned off health-data sharing altogether. In the final deck, all of that became one figure: 72% positive. It felt like the numbers and the people were describing two different products.

I haven't been able to let go of that gap. More and more software uses our own data to make decisions for us: adjusting our plans, flagging our behavior, acting before we ask. Usage can't tell you how someone relates to a system like that. A person can keep using a feature while privately wondering what it knows about them, or quietly start pulling their data back. I want to understand what people think is going on when an app uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say.

The closest I've come to studying this was sitting in on interviews. Last year I volunteered to take notes for a few sessions our UX researcher ran on AI Coach. What stayed with me was hearing people try to explain out loud what the coach was doing: building a theory as they talked, revising it, sometimes contradicting themselves. The researcher mostly let them keep going. I realized that the understanding I couldn't find in our logs was there in the room, but only because someone knew how to leave space for it. It was the most interesting part of my month, and it showed me how much skill that kind of listening takes.

I should be clear about where I'm starting. I have no publications. My research experience so far is two undergraduate projects in my HCI-track degree, an interview study and a usability test, plus what I learned by watching a good researcher work. What I do have is years of practice being careful with evidence: questioning results that look too clean and refusing to report a conclusion the data can't support. That care came to me through numbers. I want to learn it for the kinds of evidence that explain *why*: interviews, observation, and people thinking out loud.

That's why I'm applying for a PhD, and not only for research jobs. In industry, findings like the ones in that survey get noted and moved past, because the next launch is always coming. The question I care about needs room to be studied slowly and from several angles, by someone trained to do it well. I'd like to become that person.

My question will change once I'm reading the literature seriously and working with an advisor. I'm sure it begins where my current tools stop, with the people whose experience didn't fit into the 72%. I'd like to spend the next five years learning how to study them well.

AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios where information sharing violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across eight open and proprietary models, personalization improves performance, with accuracy gains of up to 11.41% using six in-context examples. However, these gains arise from different mechanisms. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 leverage semantic context to infer user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability and present trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. We present a framework to formally define and operationalize data minimization: for a given user prompt and response model, quantifying the least privacy-revealing disclosure that maintains utility, and propose a priority-queue tree search to locate this optimal point within a privacy-ordered transformation space. To date, research on these privacy concerns has been model-centered: exploring how LLMs lead to privacy risks like memorization, or can be used to infer personal characteristics about people from their content. We argue that there is a need for more research focusing on the human aspect of these privacy issues: e.g., research on how design paradigms for LLMs affect users’ disclosure behaviors, users’ mental models and preferences for privacy controls, and the design of tools, systems, and artifacts that empower end-users to reclaim ownership over their personal data. To build usable, efficient, and privacy-friendly systems powered by these models with imperfect privacy properties, our goal is to initiate discussions to outline an agenda for conducting human-centered research on privacy issues in LLM-powered systems. This Special Interest Group (SIG) aims to bring together researchers with backgrounds in usable security and privacy, human-AI collaboration, NLP, or any other related domains to share their perspectives and experiences on this problem, to help our community establish a collective understanding of the challenges, research opportunities, research methods, and strategies to collaborate with researchers outside of HCI.

CHI

“It’s a Fair Game”, or Is It? Examining How Users Navigate Disclosure Risks and Benefits When Using LLM-Based Conversational Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Michelle Jia, Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee, Bingsheng Yao, Sauvik Das, Ada Lerner, Dakuo Wang, and  Tianshi Li

In CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Apr 2024

Abs arXiv PDF Talk Website

The widespread use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based conversational agents (CAs), especially in high-stakes domains, raises many privacy concerns. Building ethical LLM-based CAs that respect user privacy requires an in-depth understanding of the privacy risks that concern users the most. However, existing research, primarily model-centered, does not provide insight into users’ perspectives. To bridge this gap, we analyzed sensitive disclosures in real-world ChatGPT conversations and conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 LLM-based CA users. We found that users are constantly faced with trade-offs between privacy, utility, and convenience when using LLM-based CAs. However, users’ erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension of the privacy risks. Additionally, the human-like interactions encouraged more sensitive disclosures, which complicated users’ ability to navigate the trade-offs. We discuss practical design guidelines and the needs for paradigmatic shifts to protect the privacy of LLM-based CA users.

IMWUT

Matcha: An IDE Plugin for Creating Accurate Privacy Nutrition Labels

Tianshi Li , Lorrie Faith Cranor, Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Apr 2024

Abs arXiv HTML Website

Apple and Google introduced their versions of privacy nutrition labels to the mobile app stores to better inform users of the apps’ data practices. However, these labels are self-reported by developers and have been found to contain many inaccuracies due to misunderstandings of the label taxonomy. In this work, we present Matcha, an IDE plugin that uses automated code analysis to help developers create accurate Google Play data safety labels. Developers can benefit from Matcha’s ability to detect user data accesses and transmissions while staying in control of the generated label by adding custom Java annotations and modifying an auto-generated XML specification. Our evaluation with 12 developers showed that Matcha helped our participants improved the accuracy of a label they created with Google’s official tool for a real-world app they developed. We found that participants preferred Matcha for its accuracy benefits. Drawing on Matcha, we discuss general design recommendations for developer tools used to create accurate standardized privacy notices.

CHI

Understanding Challenges for Developers to Create Accurate Privacy Nutrition Labels

Tianshi Li , Kayla Reiman, Yuvraj Agarwal, Lorrie Faith Cranor, and Jason I Hong

In CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Apr 2022

Best Paper Honorable Mention Award 🏅

📰 Media coverage: The Washington Post , Consumer Reports

Abs HTML PDF

Apple announced the introduction of app privacy details to their App Store in December 2020, marking the first ever real-world, large-scale deployment of the privacy nutrition label concept, which had been introduced by researchers over a decade earlier. The Apple labels are created by app developers, who self-report their app’s data practices. In this paper, we present the first study examining the usability and understandability of Apple’s privacy nutrition label creation process from the developer’s perspective. By observing and interviewing 12 iOS app developers about how they created the privacy label for a real-world app that they developed, we identified common challenges for correctly and efficiently creating privacy labels. We discuss design implications both for improving Apple’s privacy label design and for future deployment of other standardized privacy notices.

IMWUT

Honeysuckle: Annotation-Guided Code Generation of In-App Privacy Notices

Tianshi Li , Elijah B Neundorfer, Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Sep 2021

Abs HTML PDF Talk Demo

In-app privacy notices can help smartphone users make informed privacy decisions. However, they are rarely used in real-world apps, since developers often lack the knowledge, time, and resources to design and implement them well. We present Honeysuckle, a programming tool that helps Android developers build in-app privacy notices using an annotation-based code generation approach facilitated by an IDE plugin, a build system plugin, and a library. We conducted a within-subjects study with 12 Android developers to evaluate Honeysuckle. Each participant was asked to implement privacy notices for two popular open-source apps using the Honeysuckle library as a baseline as well as the annotation-based approach. Our results show that the annotation-based approach helps developers accomplish the task faster with significantly lower cognitive load. Developers preferred the annotation-based approach over the library approach because it was much easier to learn and use and allowed developers to achieve various types of privacy notices using a unified code format, which can enhance code readability and benefit team collaboration.

PMC

What makes people install a COVID-19 contact-tracing app? Understanding the influence of app design and individual difference on contact-tracing app adoption intention

Tianshi Li , Camille Cobb, Jackie (junrui) Yang, Sagar Baviskar, Yuvraj Agarwal, Beibei Li, Lujo Bauer, and Jason I Hong

Pervasive Mob. Comput. Aug 2021

Best Research Paper 2019-2021 Award 🏆

Abs HTML PDF

Smartphone-based contact-tracing apps are a promising solution to help scale up the conventional contact-tracing process. However, low adoption rates have become a major issue that prevents these apps from achieving their full potential. In this paper, we present a national-scale survey experiment (N=1963) in the U.S. to investigate the effects of app design choices and individual differences on COVID-19 contact-tracing app adoption intentions. We found that individual differences such as prosocialness, COVID-19 risk perceptions, general privacy concerns, technology readiness, and demographic factors played a more important role than app design choices such as decentralized design vs. centralized design, location use, app providers, and the presentation of security risks. Certain app designs could exacerbate the different preferences in different sub-populations which may lead to an inequality of acceptance to certain app design choices (e.g., developed by state health authorities vs. a large tech company) among different groups of people (e.g., people living in rural areas vs. people living in urban areas). Our mediation analysis showed that one’s perception of the public health benefits offered by the app and the adoption willingness of other people had a larger effect in explaining the observed effects of app design choices and individual differences than one’s perception of the app’s security and privacy risks. With these findings, we discuss practical implications on the design, marketing, and deployment of COVID-19 contact-tracing apps in the U.S.

CSCW

How Developers Talk About Personal Data and What It Means for User Privacy: A Case Study of a Developer Forum on Reddit

Tianshi Li , Elizabeth Louie, Laura Dabbish, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Hum. Comput. Interact. Jan 2021

Abs HTML PDF Talk

While online developer forums are major resources of knowledge for application developers, their roles in promoting better privacy practices remain underexplored. In this paper, we conducted a qualitative analysis of a sample of 207 threads (4772 unique posts) mentioning different forms of personal data from the /r/androiddev forum on Reddit. We started with bottom-up open coding on the sampled posts to develop a typology of discussions about personal data use and conducted follow-up analyses to understand what types of posts elicited in-depth discussions on privacy issues or mentioned risky data practices. Our results show that Android developers rarely discussed privacy concerns when talking about a specific app design or implementation problem, but often had active discussions around privacy when stimulated by certain external events representing new privacy-enhancing restrictions from the Android operating system, app store policies, or privacy laws. Developers often felt these restrictions could cause considerable cost yet fail to generate any compelling benefit for themselves. Given these results, we present a set of suggestions for Android OS and the app store to design more effective methods to enhance privacy, and for developer forums(e.g., /r/androiddev) to encourage more in-depth privacy discussions and nudge developers to think more about privacy.

IMWUT

Coconut: An IDE Plugin for Developing Privacy-Friendly Apps

Tianshi Li , Yuvraj Agarwal, and Jason I Hong

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Dec 2018

Abs HTML PDF Demo Website

Although app developers are responsible for protecting users’ privacy, this task can be very challenging. In this paper, we present Coconut, an Android Studio plugin that helps developers handle privacy requirements by engaging developers to think about privacy during the development process and providing real-time feedback on potential privacy issues. We start by presenting new findings based on a series of semi-structured interviews with Android developers, probing into the difficulties with privacy that developers face when building apps. Based on these findings, we implemented a proof-of-concept prototype of Coconut and evaluated it in a controlled lab study with 18 Android developers (including eight professional developers). Our study results suggest that apps developed with Coconut handled privacy concerns better, and the developers that used Coconut had a better understanding of their code’s behavior and wrote a better privacy policy for their app. We also found that requiring developers to do a small amount of annotating work regarding their apps’ personal data practices during the development process may result in a significant improvement in app privacy.
